items.title: 1.8.1 Method of Constructing the Graph of an Inverse Function

blocks.text: The graph of an inverse function is obtained geometrically as follows:

items: (i) Draw the graph of the given one-to-one function.
(ii) Consider the line \(y = x\) on the same coordinate plane.
(iii) Reflect the graph of the function about the line \(y = x\).
(iv) The resulting reflected curve represents the graph of the inverse function.

blocks.text: The reflection ensures that each point on the original graph is mapped to a corresponding point on the inverse graph by maintaining equal perpendicular distance from the line \(y = x\), preserving the geometric symmetry between the two graphs.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In practice, reflecting in \(y = x\) is easy: swap the coordinates. The point \((p, q)\) goes to \((q, p)\).
Why this is a true mirror image: the midpoint \(\left(\frac{p+q}{2}, \frac{p+q}{2}\right)\) lies on \(y = x\), and the segment from \((p, q)\) to \((q, p)\) has slope \(-1\), perpendicular to \(y = x\). So both points are at equal perpendicular distance from the line, as the book says.
Special features also move: an intercept on one axis becomes an intercept on the other, and a horizontal asymptote becomes a vertical one.

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem: (Logarithmic Graph from Exponential Graph) Show graphically that the function \(y = \ln x\) is the inverse of the function \(y = e^{x}\).
steps:
Given: the exponential function \(y = e^{x}\).
To prove: graphically, that \(y = \ln x\) is its inverse.
Method: 1.8.1. First confirm that \(y = e^{x}\) is one-to-one (so an inverse exists), then reflect its graph in the line \(y = x\) and identify the reflected curve.

Step 1: The function is invertible
Consider the exponential function \(y = e^{x}\). Note that the function \(y = e^{x}\) is one to one on \(]-\infty, \infty[\) and its range is \(]0, \infty[\). Hence, it is invertible and its inverse is defined on \(]0, \infty[\).
Why: 1.8 says an inverse exists for a one-to-one function (with co-domain = range). The range of \(e^{x}\) becomes the domain of the inverse.

Step 2: Draw \(y = e^{x}\) and the line \(y = x\)
We draw the graph of \(y = e^{x}\) along with the line \(y = x\) (see Figure 1.13). Some points of \(y = e^{x}\) (values rounded):
\[x = -2,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2\]
\[e^{x} \approx 0.14,\ 0.37,\ 1,\ 2.72,\ 7.39\]
Why: step (i) and (ii) of the method: the graph of the function and the mirror line on the same axes.

Step 3: Reflect the points about y = x
To obtain the graph of the inverse function, points on the curve \(y = e^{x}\) are reflected about the line \(y = x\). Reflecting in \(y = x\) swaps the coordinates:
\[(-2,\ 0.14) \to (0.14,\ -2)\]
\[(-1,\ 0.37) \to (0.37,\ -1)\]
\[(0,\ 1) \to (1,\ 0)\]
\[(1,\ 2.72) \to (2.72,\ 1)\]
\[(2,\ 7.39) \to (7.39,\ 2)\]
Why: step (iii). The point \((p, q)\) and its image \((q, p)\) have their midpoint on \(y = x\) and the segment between them is perpendicular to \(y = x\), so both are the same distance from the line (the dashed segments in Figure 1.13).

Step 4: Join the reflected points
The curve passing through these reflected points is then drawn (see Figure 1.13). The resulting curve represents the function:
\[y = \ln x\]
which is clearly defined on the interval \(]0, \infty[\).
Why: step (iv). Every reflected point \((e^{p}, p)\) satisfies \(y = \ln x\), because \(\ln(e^{p}) = p\).

Check:
From the table: \(\ln 1 = 0\), \(\ln 2.72 \approx 1\), \(\ln 0.37 \approx -1\), \(\ln 7.39 \approx 2\). Algebraically, interchanging \(x\) and \(y\) in \(y = e^{x}\) gives \(x = e^{y}\), i.e. \(y = \ln x\). The features also swap: \(e^{x}\) has horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) and point \((0, 1)\); \(\ln x\) has vertical asymptote \(x = 0\) and point \((1, 0)\).
blocks.answer: The reflection of the graph of \(y = e^{x}\) in the line \(y = x\) is the graph of \(y = \ln x\). Hence, the function \(y = \ln x\) is the inverse of \(y = e^{x}\).

blocks.alt: The curve y = e to the power x, the line y = x and the curve y = ln x on axes from minus 5 to 5. Points on y = e to the power x are joined by dashed segments, perpendicular to y = x, to their mirror points on y = ln x; for example (0, 1) is joined to (1, 0) and (1, 2.72) to (2.72, 1).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.13: y = ln x as the reflection of y = e^x in the line y = x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. To graph \(f^{-1}\): draw \(f\), draw \(y = x\), reflect, and the image is \(f^{-1}\).
2. Reflection in \(y = x\) means \((p, q) \to (q, p)\).
3. \(y = \ln x\) is the reflection of \(y = e^{x}\): \((0, 1) \to (1, 0)\), asymptote \(y = 0 \to x = 0\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reflecting a function that is not one-to-one (e.g. \(|x|\) or \(x^{2}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\)): the mirror image is then not the graph of a function.
2. Drawing \(\ln x\) for \(x \le 0\) or letting it cross the \(y\)-axis.
3. Moving points straight across horizontally or vertically instead of perpendicular to \(y = x\).
